item.title: ARM Architecture Introduction
item.description:
Arm defines a family of instruction set architectures (ISAs), not one processor implementation. The architecture specifies programmer-visible state, instruction semantics, exceptions, privilege, and memory ordering. A core’s pipeline, cache hierarchy, and branch predictor are microarchitectural choices.

Architecture profiles separate deployment requirements. A-profile targets application processors with virtual memory, R-profile targets real-time systems, and M-profile targets microcontrollers. The execution states and privilege model below describe A-profile systems unless stated otherwise.

Execution States and Instruction Sets #

AArch32 provides 32-bit general-purpose registers and can execute the A32 instruction set or the variable-length T32 instruction set historically called Thumb. AArch64, introduced by Armv8-A, provides thirty-one 64-bit general-purpose registers and the fixed-width A64 instruction set. X0 through X30 name the 64-bit registers; W0 through W30 name their low 32 bits. Writing a W register clears the upper half of its corresponding X register.

item.title: RISC-V Architecture Introduction
item.description:
RISC-V is an open instruction set architecture organized as a base integer ISA plus separately versioned extensions. The ISA defines instruction behavior and privileged execution; a platform profile, ABI, and execution environment add the requirements needed to run interoperable software.

Base Integer ISA and Register Convention #

RV32I and RV64I provide 32-bit and 64-bit integer registers respectively. Both define thirty-two general-purpose registers, x0 through x31. x0 always reads as zero and discards writes. The program counter is architecturally visible through control-flow effects rather than as a general-purpose register.

item.title: x86 and x86-64 Architecture Overview
item.description:
x86 began with Intel’s 16-bit 8086. The 80286 introduced protected mode, IA-32 established the 32-bit programming model and paging, and AMD64 extended the architecture to 64-bit execution. Intel calls the combined architecture Intel 64 and IA-32; AMD documentation uses AMD64. Vendor names do not determine every feature, so software must discover extensions explicitly.

item.title: CPU Architecture Overview
item.description:
A processor implements an instruction set architecture (ISA): the contract that defines instructions, registers, data types, address formation, exceptions, and privilege behavior. A microarchitecture implements that contract with pipelines, execution units, caches, predictors, and internal queues. Programs observe architectural state; performance depends on microarchitectural state.

From Fetch to Retirement #

At a conceptual level, a processor fetches instruction bytes, decodes an instruction, obtains operands, executes the operation, accesses memory when required, and commits the result. A simple processor can perform those steps sequentially. A pipelined processor overlaps steps from several instructions, thus improving throughput without requiring every instruction to have low latency.
